title: Machine learning for risk profiling: An analysis of pension fund participants
tldr: Using 81,563 Turkish pension fund participants, boosting methods (LightGBM R²=0.167) modestly outperform the regulatory benchmark (R²=0.131) for predicting actual portfolio risk, with just four variables (self-reported risk attitude, lottery choice, age, age-squared) achieving comparable performance to the full questionnaire.
problem_and_motivation: Pension systems worldwide face a tension between accurate risk assessment and operational efficiency. Long, complex risk questionnaires create 'participant friction' leading to low completion rates. Standard questionnaires show limited ability to predict actual investment behavior (typically R² of 0.10-0.15). This study examines whether ML can improve risk profiling accuracy while identifying the minimum variables needed for effective assessment.
approach: Analysis of 81,563 individual investors from a major Turkish pension fund company (2018-2022). Portfolio risk calculated as weighted average of fund risk scores (1-7 scale based on 5-year volatility). Compared 10 ML models (OLS, Ridge, Lasso, Elastic Net, KNN, CART, ANN, Random Forest, GBoost, XGBoost, LightGBM) against the regulatory benchmark using 20-fold cross-validation. Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) identified most important predictors. Age-squared added to linear models to capture nonlinearity.
findings: Self-reported risk attitude (Q3) was the most important predictor across all models. Age showed a non-linear inverted-U relationship with risk-taking, peaking at age 35-44. Four variables (Q3, Q4, age, age-squared) achieved comparable performance to the full 7-question set. LightGBM achieved R²=0.167 vs. regulatory benchmark R²=0.131 (27% relative improvement). Even with 4 variables, models outperformed the full regulatory benchmark. Overall R² remained modest (0.13-0.17), consistent with prior risk preference literature.

definitions: Portfolio Risk: Weighted average of fund risk scores based on 5-year annualized weekly return volatility
Risk Profiling: Classification of investors into risk groups (low/medium/high/very high) based on questionnaire responses
Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE): Iterative method that ranks and prunes features based on model performance
CMB Risk Questionnaire: Standardized Turkish regulatory tool with 7 core questions assessing risk attitudes
Participant Friction: Barriers to survey completion caused by lengthy, complex questionnaires

topic_relevance.mapping_rationale: Core contribution is predictive modelling of investment risk profiles using multiple ML algorithms with cross-validation
Compares 10 ML models including boosting methods, random forest, neural networks against regulatory benchmarks
Risk profiling is analogous to credit scoring—classifying individuals into risk categories for financial product suitability, though applied to investment risk rather than credit default

limitations: Dataset from single Turkish pension fund may not generalize to other regulatory/cultural contexts
Cross-sectional design does not capture temporal evolution of risk preferences
Overall R² remains modest (0.13-0.17), suggesting significant unobserved determinants
Portfolio risk may be influenced by advisor recommendations and defaults, not just preferences
Boosting models have opacity concerns for regulatory acceptance despite higher accuracy
remember_this: Key finding: just 4 variables (self-reported risk attitude, lottery choice, age, age-squared) achieve comparable performance to the full 7-question regulatory questionnaire. The non-linear inverted-U relationship between age and risk-taking is critical—simple linear models miss this lifecycle pattern. Even the best ML models explain only 13-17% of portfolio risk variance, consistent with the inherent difficulty of predicting financial risk-taking behavior.
